rationale: B wins because it knows when to stop. Its refusal of "Data sovereignty: compliance teams get an AI model that keeps data in-house" is the adult move: without a named regulated customer, that is a costume change on the closed-API fight, not a fourth story. A is strong, but "For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody, not capability" keeps a borderline duplicate alive and leans on verticals the update never supplied.
gaps_in_A: "For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody, not capability" names banks and hospitals even though the update only says regulated enterprises. It can work, but it needs a customer before it deserves its own lane.

"The protagonist is the regulated buyer" is too close to angle 2's "regulated customers" unless the team can produce a named buyer or regulator. Without that, it is the same story in different clothes.
"The prevailing belief: proprietary frontier models are the core asset" is an external market thesis, not a supplied fact. It needs evidence or softer framing before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "Data sovereignty: compliance teams get an AI model that keeps data in-house" may be too quickly killed as `duplicate`; with a named regulated customer or regulator, that becomes a real vertical trade angle.

"buyers who cannot send data outside their own environment" is a plausible regulated-enterprise constraint, but the update gives Databricks' positioning, not a verified buyer constraint. Phrase it as a claim until sourced.
"enterprise-AI procurement reporter" is specific but a little desk-fantasy. Stronger outlet shape would separate enterprise AI business press from banking or healthcare IT trades.
